facts.s: Bhutan measures national progress with an index called Gross National Happiness.
facts.e: Bhutan's government uses Gross National Happiness, which weighs wellbeing, culture, environment and good governance alongside economic growth.

facts.s: In Bulgaria, nodding your head up and down traditionally means "no".
facts.e: In Bulgaria (and parts of Albania and Greece), the meanings of nodding and shaking the head are traditionally reversed compared with most of the world.

facts.s: Iceland has no standing army.
facts.e: Iceland is a NATO member but has no army of its own. Its defence relies on its Coast Guard, a peacekeeping unit and agreements with allies.

facts.s: Costa Rica abolished its army in 1948.
facts.e: After a short civil war, President José Figueres Ferrer abolished the military in 1948, and the 1949 constitution made it permanent. The money went to education and healthcare instead.

facts.s: In Japan, leaving a tip at a restaurant is expected, as in the USA.
facts.e: Tipping is uncommon in Japan. Good service is considered part of the job, and staff may even chase you to return money you left behind.

facts.s: Finland has an estimated 3 million saunas for a population of about 5.5 million people.
facts.e: The sauna is central to Finnish life. There are saunas in homes, offices, and even the Finnish parliament.

facts.s: The Great Wall of China is visible from the Moon with the naked eye.
facts.e: The wall is very long but only a few metres wide. From the Moon, about 384,000 km away, it is far too narrow to see. Even from low Earth orbit it is extremely hard to spot.

facts.s: Nepal's national flag is the only national flag that is not a rectangle.
facts.e: Nepal's flag is made of two stacked pennants (triangles). Its constitution even includes precise geometric instructions for drawing it.

facts.s: In Spain, people traditionally eat 12 grapes at midnight on New Year's Eve, one with each chime of the clock.
facts.e: The Twelve Grapes tradition is meant to bring good luck for each month of the new year. Many people watch the clock in Madrid's Puerta del Sol on TV.

facts.s: During the Indian festival of Holi, people throw brightly coloured powder and water at each other.
facts.e: Holi celebrates the arrival of spring and the victory of good over evil. It's celebrated across India and Nepal, and increasingly worldwide.

facts.s: The traditional Ethiopian calendar has 13 months.
facts.e: It has 12 months of 30 days plus a 13th month, Pagume, of 5 or 6 days. It also runs about 7 to 8 years behind the Gregorian calendar.

facts.s: In Saudi Arabia, the weekend falls on Friday and Saturday.
facts.e: Saudi Arabia moved its weekend from Thursday–Friday to Friday–Saturday in 2013. Friday is the main day of congregational prayer in Islam.

facts.s: Sydney is the capital of Australia.
facts.e: The capital is Canberra, a planned city chosen as a compromise between rivals Sydney and Melbourne. Parliament first met there in 1927.

facts.s: South Korea officially switched to the international way of counting age in 2023.
facts.e: Traditionally a baby was counted as 1 year old at birth and everyone aged a year on New Year's Day. A 2023 law made international age the standard for official use.

facts.s: Denmark's flag is often cited as the oldest national flag still in continuous use.
facts.e: Legend says the Dannebrog fell from the sky during a battle in 1219. Its design has been in use since at least the 14th century.

facts.s: Mongolia is the most sparsely populated sovereign country in the world.
facts.e: With about 2 people per square kilometre, Mongolia has the lowest population density of any independent country. Around 30% of Mongolians are nomadic or semi-nomadic.

facts.s: In Thailand, touching someone's head is usually considered rude.
facts.e: The head is traditionally seen as the most sacred part of the body, while pointing your feet at people or religious images is considered disrespectful.

facts.s: Vatican City is the smallest country in the world by area.
facts.e: Vatican City covers about 0.49 km², smaller than many city parks, and has a population of only a few hundred people.

facts.s: Russia spans five time zones.
facts.e: Russia spans 11 time zones, from Kaliningrad in the west to Kamchatka in the far east.

facts.s: The Maldives is the world's lowest-lying country, with an average ground level of about 1.5 metres above sea level.
facts.e: This makes the Maldives one of the countries most threatened by rising sea levels.

facts.s: Bananas are slightly radioactive.
facts.e: Bananas contain potassium, a tiny fraction of which is radioactive potassium-40. The dose is harmless, and the 'banana equivalent dose' is used as a light-hearted unit of radiation.

facts.s: Properly sealed honey can stay edible for an extremely long time.
facts.e: Honey has very little water and is acidic, so most bacteria and moulds can't grow in it. It may crystallise, but that doesn't mean it has gone bad.

facts.s: Botanically, a tomato is a vegetable.
facts.e: Botanically, tomatoes are fruits, specifically berries, because they develop from a flower and contain seeds. In cooking they are treated as vegetables.

facts.s: Peanuts are not true nuts; they are legumes, related to beans and peas.
facts.e: Peanuts grow underground in pods, like other legumes. Botanically, 'nuts' are hard-shelled fruits like hazelnuts and chestnuts.

facts.s: Most "wasabi" served outside Japan is actually horseradish dyed green.
facts.e: Real wasabi is rare and expensive to grow, so most restaurant wasabi is a mix of horseradish, mustard and green colouring.

facts.s: Fortune cookies are a traditional dessert in China.
facts.e: Fortune cookies became popular in the United States in the early 20th century and are thought to come from Japanese crackers. They are rarely seen in China.

facts.s: Cashew nuts grow attached to the bottom of a fruit called the cashew apple.
facts.e: Each cashew nut hangs below a juicy 'cashew apple'. The shell contains an irritating oil, so cashews are always sold shelled and processed.

facts.s: Saffron, made from the stigmas of crocus flowers, is one of the most expensive spices in the world by weight.
facts.e: Every flower yields only three thin stigmas, each picked by hand. It takes roughly 150,000 flowers to make a kilogram of saffron.

facts.s: The holes in Swiss cheese are made by mice nibbling it while it ages.
facts.e: The holes ('eyes') come from carbon dioxide bubbles released by bacteria during ripening. Tiny hay particles in the milk also help the bubbles form.

facts.s: Potatoes were first domesticated in the Andes of South America.
facts.e: Potatoes were domesticated in what is now southern Peru and north-western Bolivia thousands of years ago. They reached Europe only in the 16th century.

facts.s: The croissant descends from the Austrian kipferl.
facts.e: The croissant is a symbol of France, but it grew out of the Viennese kipferl, popularised by Viennese bakeries in Paris in the 1830s and 40s.

facts.s: Coffee beans are the seeds of a fruit.
facts.e: Coffee 'beans' are the seeds inside the red or purple fruit of the coffee plant, often called coffee cherries.

facts.s: Traditional Italian carbonara is made with cream.
facts.e: Traditional carbonara uses egg, hard cheese (pecorino or parmesan), cured pork (guanciale) and black pepper. The creaminess comes from the eggs and cheese.

facts.s: White chocolate contains lots of cocoa solids.
facts.e: White chocolate is made from cocoa butter, sugar and milk. It contains no cocoa solids, which is why it isn't brown.

facts.s: Chocolate (cacao) was first used in Mesoamerica, where it was often drunk as a bitter beverage.
facts.e: The Olmec, Maya and Aztec peoples drank cacao, often spiced and unsweetened. Cacao beans were even used as a currency by the Aztecs.

facts.s: Singapore has banned the sale of chewing gum since 1992.
facts.e: The ban was introduced partly because discarded gum was damaging public places and train doors. Therapeutic gum, such as nicotine gum, is allowed from pharmacies.
facts.w: Chewing gum sales ban in Singapore

facts.s: In Switzerland, owning just one guinea pig is not allowed, because they are social animals.
facts.e: Swiss animal welfare law requires social animals like guinea pigs to be kept with companions of their own kind.

facts.s: In Germany, most shops are legally required to close on Sundays.
facts.e: Sundays and public holidays are protected as days of rest. There are exceptions for bakeries, petrol stations, train stations and some special shopping Sundays.

facts.s: Estonia was the first country to use internet voting in legally binding nationwide elections.
facts.e: Estonians could first vote online in the 2005 local elections, using their national digital ID cards. Today a large share of votes is cast online.

facts.s: Voting in federal elections is compulsory for adult citizens in Australia.
facts.e: Since 1924, Australian citizens aged 18 and over must enrol and vote. Turnout is usually above 90%.

facts.s: Most countries in the world drive on the left side of the road.
facts.e: Only about a third of countries drive on the left, including the UK, India, Japan and Australia. Most countries drive on the right.

facts.s: New Zealand was the first self-governing country to give women the right to vote in national elections.
facts.e: New Zealand women won the vote in 1893 after a campaign led by Kate Sheppard, whose portrait appears on the NZ$10 note.

facts.s: Japan lowered its legal age of adulthood from 20 to 18 in 2022.
facts.e: Since April 2022, 18-year-olds in Japan can sign contracts and marry without parental consent. The drinking and smoking age stays at 20.

facts.s: In Sweden, the law lets anyone walk, and even camp for a night, on most private land, as long as they respect nature and owners.
facts.e: This 'right of public access' (allemansrätten) is a deep Nordic tradition. Norway and Finland have similar rights.

facts.s: France has a law giving many employees a 'right to disconnect' from work emails outside working hours.
facts.e: Since 2017, French companies with 50 or more employees must agree on rules that protect workers from out-of-hours emails and messages.

facts.s: Papua New Guinea has more living languages than any other country, over 800.
facts.e: Its rugged mountains and isolated valleys allowed hundreds of languages to develop separately. Tok Pisin, English and Hiri Motu are widely used to bridge them.

facts.s: India's constitution officially recognises 22 'scheduled' languages.
facts.e: The Eighth Schedule lists 22 languages, including Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Marathi and Urdu. Hundreds more are spoken across the country.
facts.w: Eighth Schedule to the Constitution of India

facts.s: Spanish has more native speakers than any other language.
facts.e: Mandarin Chinese has the most native speakers, about 900 million or more. Spanish is second, with nearly 500 million. English has the most total speakers when second-language speakers are counted.
facts.w: List of languages by number of native speakers

facts.s: On La Gomera in the Canary Islands, people use a whistled language called Silbo Gomero.
facts.e: Silbo turns Spanish into whistles that can carry across deep valleys for several kilometres. It's taught in local schools and is recognised by UNESCO.

facts.s: The Korean alphabet, Hangul, was deliberately invented in the 15th century.
facts.e: King Sejong the Great and his scholars created Hangul in 1443 so ordinary people could read and write easily. Korea celebrates Hangul Day every October.

facts.s: The word 'robot' was first used in a Czech play.
facts.e: It comes from Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R. and the Czech word 'robota', meaning forced labour. His brother Josef suggested the word.

facts.s: The Hawaiian alphabet has only 13 letters.
facts.e: It has 5 vowels and 8 consonants, including the ʻokina, a glottal stop. Words like 'aloha' and 'ukulele' come from Hawaiian.

facts.s: Basque is a language isolate, unrelated to any other living language.
facts.e: Basque, spoken in parts of Spain and France, is thought to predate the arrival of Indo-European languages in Europe. Its origins remain a mystery.

facts.s: Esperanto is the official language of several countries.
facts.e: Esperanto was invented in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof as an easy international language. It has an active community worldwide, but no country uses it as an official language.

facts.s: English words like 'shampoo', 'bungalow' and 'jungle' come from Indian languages.
facts.e: Shampoo comes from Hindi 'chāmpo' (to press or massage), bungalow from 'bangla' (Bengal-style house), and jungle from 'jangal'.
facts.w: List of English words of Hindi or Urdu origin

facts.s: Arabic is written from right to left, but its numbers are read from left to right.
facts.e: Arabic text runs right to left, but multi-digit numbers are written with the most significant digit on the left, just as in English.

facts.s: In Mandarin Chinese, the same syllable can mean completely different things depending on its tone.
facts.e: Mandarin has four main tones. For example, 'mā' can mean 'mother' while 'mǎ' can mean 'horse'.

facts.s: Sign language is universal, so deaf people everywhere use the same signs.
facts.e: There are hundreds of sign languages. British Sign Language and American Sign Language are very different, even though both countries mostly speak English.

facts.s: Finnish and Hungarian are distantly related languages.
facts.e: Both belong to the Uralic language family, along with Estonian. Unlike most European languages, they are not Indo-European.

facts.s: Russia's land area is larger than the entire surface area of Pluto.
facts.e: Russia covers about 17.1 million km², and Pluto's whole surface is about 16.7 million km².

facts.s: Africa is the only continent crossed by both the Equator and the Prime Meridian.
facts.e: The Equator and the Prime Meridian meet in the Gulf of Guinea, off the coast of West Africa.

facts.s: Mount Everest is the tallest mountain on Earth when measured from base to peak.
facts.e: Everest has the highest summit above sea level, at 8,849 m. Measured from its base on the ocean floor, Hawaii's Mauna Kea is about 10,200 m tall.

facts.s: Canada has the longest coastline of any country.
facts.e: Thanks to its thousands of Arctic islands, Canada's coastline is over 200,000 km long by common measures, far more than any other country.

facts.s: The shores of the Dead Sea are the lowest land on Earth, about 430 metres below sea level.
facts.e: The Dead Sea is also so salty that people float effortlessly in it. Its level has been dropping for decades.

facts.s: The Sahara is the largest desert in the world.
facts.e: A desert is defined by low rainfall, not heat. Antarctica is the largest desert, followed by the Arctic. The Sahara is the largest hot desert.

facts.s: Russia's Lake Baikal holds about a fifth of the world's unfrozen surface fresh water.
facts.e: Baikal is the deepest lake on Earth, at over 1,600 m, and one of the oldest, at about 25 million years.

facts.s: France has more time zones than any other country.
facts.e: Because of overseas territories like French Polynesia, Réunion and New Caledonia, France spans 12 time zones (13 including its Antarctic claim).

facts.s: Istanbul is a city on two continents, Europe and Asia.
facts.e: The Bosphorus strait divides Istanbul between Europe and Asia, and millions of people cross between the two every day.

facts.s: Brazil borders every South American country except Chile and Ecuador.
facts.e: Brazil is so large that it touches 10 of the other 12 South American countries, plus French Guiana.

facts.s: The Danube flows through or along more countries than any other river: 10.
facts.e: It passes Germany, Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, Moldova and Ukraine, and four capital cities.

facts.s: Indonesia is made up of more than 17,000 islands.
facts.e: Indonesia is the world's largest archipelagic country. About 6,000 of its islands are inhabited.

facts.s: There's a point in the South Pacific so far from land that the nearest humans are often astronauts on the International Space Station.
facts.e: Point Nemo, the oceanic pole of inaccessibility, is about 2,700 km from the nearest land. The ISS, about 400 km up, is often closer.

facts.s: Alaska is both the westernmost and the easternmost US state.
facts.e: Alaska's Aleutian Islands cross the 180° meridian, so some of them lie in the Eastern Hemisphere.

facts.s: The Equator passes through India.
facts.e: India lies entirely north of the Equator. It's the Tropic of Cancer that crosses India, through eight states.

facts.s: Lightning never strikes the same place twice.
facts.e: Lightning often strikes tall objects repeatedly. The Empire State Building is hit around 20 to 25 times a year.

facts.s: Water expands when it freezes, which is why ice floats.
facts.e: As water freezes, its molecules form an open hexagonal lattice that takes up about 9% more space. Lakes freeze from the top down, which protects the life below.

facts.s: Old church windows are thicker at the bottom because glass slowly flows downward over centuries.
facts.e: Glass at room temperature doesn't flow measurably. Old panes were uneven because of how they were made, and glaziers often put the thicker edge at the bottom.

facts.s: Sound travels about four times faster in water than in air.
facts.e: Sound moves at about 343 m/s in air and roughly 1,480 m/s in water, because water's molecules are packed much more closely.

facts.s: Helium is the only element that won't freeze solid at normal pressure, no matter how cold it gets.
facts.e: Even near absolute zero, helium stays liquid unless it's squeezed to about 25 times atmospheric pressure.

facts.s: Early humans lived alongside the dinosaurs.
facts.e: Non-bird dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago. Our species appeared only about 300,000 years ago. Birds, however, are living dinosaurs.

facts.s: Diamonds and the graphite in pencils are made of the same element.
facts.e: Both are pure carbon. In diamond the atoms form a rigid 3D lattice. In graphite they form sheets that slide over each other.

facts.s: The Eiffel Tower can grow about 15 cm taller in summer.
facts.e: Iron expands when it heats up, so the tower's height varies by around 15 cm with the temperature.

facts.s: Absolute zero, −273.15 °C, is the lowest temperature possible.
facts.e: At absolute zero, particles would have the minimum possible energy. Scientists have cooled atoms to within billionths of a degree of it, but never reached it.

facts.s: Different areas of the tongue detect different tastes: sweet at the tip, bitter at the back.
facts.e: The 'tongue map' came from a mistranslation of a 1901 German paper. Every area of the tongue that has taste buds can detect all basic tastes.

facts.s: The air we breathe is mostly oxygen.
facts.e: Earth's atmosphere is about 78% nitrogen and only about 21% oxygen, with argon, carbon dioxide and other gases making up the rest.

facts.s: A lightning bolt can be about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
facts.e: Lightning can heat the air to around 30,000 °C, while the Sun's visible surface is about 5,500 °C.

facts.s: Water can boil at room temperature if the air pressure is low enough.
facts.e: A liquid's boiling point drops with pressure. That's why water boils at around 70 °C on top of Mount Everest.

facts.s: Albert Einstein failed mathematics at school.
facts.e: This is a popular myth. Einstein excelled at maths and had mastered calculus by about age 15.

facts.s: Antibiotics are effective against the viruses that cause colds and flu.
facts.e: Antibiotics only work against bacteria. Using them for viral infections doesn't help and contributes to antibiotic resistance.

facts.s: A day on Venus is longer than its year.
facts.e: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to spin once, but only about 225 Earth days to orbit the Sun. It also spins backwards compared with most planets.

facts.s: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth.
facts.e: The Sun is about 150 million km away. If it suddenly vanished, we wouldn't notice for about 8 minutes.

facts.s: There is no gravity on the International Space Station.
facts.e: Gravity at the ISS's height is about 90% as strong as on the ground. Astronauts float because they're in constant free fall around Earth.

facts.s: The footprints left on the Moon by Apollo astronauts could last for millions of years.
facts.e: The Moon has no wind or water to erase them. Only slow erosion from tiny meteorite impacts will eventually wear them away.

facts.s: Saturn is less dense than water.
facts.e: Saturn's average density is about 0.69 g/cm³, lower than water's 1 g/cm³. In a big enough bathtub, it would float.

facts.s: Olympus Mons on Mars is about two and a half times as tall as Mount Everest.
facts.e: This shield volcano rises about 22 km and is roughly as wide as France. It's one of the largest volcanoes in the Solar System.

facts.s: Seen from space, the Sun is yellow.
facts.e: The Sun emits all visible colours and appears white from space. It looks yellow from Earth because our atmosphere scatters the blue light.

facts.s: Some neutron stars spin hundreds of times per second.
facts.e: Neutron stars are city-sized remains of exploded stars. The fastest known spins about 716 times a second.

facts.s: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a giant storm that has been observed for nearly 200 years.
facts.e: It has been observed continuously since at least 1831. The storm is wider than Earth, though it has been shrinking.

facts.s: In 2023, India's Chandrayaan-3 became the first mission to land near the Moon's south pole.
facts.e: Its Vikram lander touched down on 23 August 2023, a region of interest because it may contain water ice.

facts.s: Mercury is the hottest planet because it's closest to the Sun.
facts.e: Venus is the hottest planet, at about 465 °C, because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat. Mercury has almost no atmosphere and is freezing on its night side.

facts.s: Voyager 1, launched in 1977, is the most distant human-made object.
facts.e: It entered interstellar space in 2012 and is now more than 24 billion km away. Its signals take over 22 hours to reach us.

facts.s: More than a million Earths could fit inside the Sun.
facts.e: The Sun's volume is about 1.3 million times Earth's. It holds 99.8% of the mass in the Solar System.

facts.s: Astronauts can grow slightly taller while living in space.
facts.e: Without gravity compressing the spine, astronauts can grow up to about 3% taller. They shrink back after returning to Earth.
facts.w: Effect of spaceflight on the human body

facts.s: The first person in space was Yuri Gagarin, in 1961.
facts.e: On 12 April 1961 he orbited Earth once in Vostok 1, a flight of 108 minutes.

facts.s: Humans use only 10% of their brains.
facts.e: Brain scans show activity throughout the brain, and almost every area has a known function. Even during sleep, many areas stay active.
facts.w: Ten percent of the brain myth

facts.s: Babies are born with more bones than adults have.
facts.e: Newborns have around 270 to 300 bones. Many fuse together during growth, leaving adults with 206.

facts.s: The cells lining your stomach are replaced every few days.
facts.e: The stomach's surface cells are constantly renewed, and a layer of mucus protects them from the strong acid that digests food.

facts.s: Hair and fingernails keep growing after death.
facts.e: After death the skin dries and pulls back, which makes hair and nails look longer. Growth needs living cells and stops.

facts.s: Most stomach ulcers are caused by a bacterium, not by stress.
facts.e: Barry Marshall and Robin Warren showed that Helicobacter pylori causes most ulcers. Marshall even drank a culture of it, and they won the 2005 Nobel Prize.

facts.s: Your heart beats about 100,000 times a day.
facts.e: At around 70 beats per minute, that's roughly 100,000 beats a day and nearly 3 billion over a lifetime.

facts.s: Cracking your knuckles causes arthritis.
facts.e: Studies have found no link. One doctor cracked the knuckles of only one hand for over 60 years and found no difference between his hands.

facts.s: The smallest bone in the human body is in the ear.
facts.e: The stapes, or stirrup, in the middle ear is about 3 mm long. It passes sound vibrations to the inner ear.

facts.s: Blood in your veins is blue until it touches oxygen.
facts.e: Blood is always red: bright red when oxygen-rich and darker red when not. Veins look blue because of how light passes through skin.

facts.s: The cornea of your eye has no blood vessels and gets much of its oxygen directly from the air.
facts.e: Blood vessels would block your vision, so the cornea absorbs oxygen dissolved in the tear film from the air.

facts.s: Even identical twins have different fingerprints.
facts.e: Fingerprints form in the womb, shaped by genes and by tiny differences in pressure, position and the surrounding fluid.

facts.s: Shaving makes hair grow back thicker and darker.
facts.e: Shaving cuts hair at a blunt angle, which can feel coarser, but it doesn't change thickness, colour or growth rate.

facts.s: The human liver can regrow after a large part of it is removed.
facts.e: The liver can regenerate to its full size even after much of it is removed, which makes living-donor liver transplants possible.

facts.s: You lose most of your body heat through your head.
facts.e: The head loses heat at about the same rate as any other uncovered part of the body. The myth came from a flawed military experiment.

facts.s: Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood.
facts.e: Two hearts pump blood to the gills and one to the rest of the body. Their blood uses copper-based haemocyanin, which makes it blue.

facts.s: Bulls charge because the colour red makes them angry.
facts.e: Cattle can't distinguish red from green well. Bulls react to the movement of the cape, not its colour.

facts.s: A group of flamingos is called a 'flamboyance'.
facts.e: Flamingos get their pink colour from pigments in the algae and shrimp they eat.

facts.s: Goldfish have a memory of only three seconds.
facts.e: Experiments show goldfish can remember things for months, and they can be trained to respond to sounds, colours and lights.

facts.s: One jellyfish species can turn back into an earlier stage of its life, making it biologically 'immortal'.
facts.e: When stressed or injured, Turritopsis dohrnii can revert from adult to polyp and start its life cycle again.

facts.s: Sea otters often hold paws while they sleep so they don't drift apart.
facts.e: Sea otters rest floating on their backs, often in groups called rafts, and may wrap themselves in kelp to stay anchored.

facts.s: Wombats produce cube-shaped poop.
facts.e: The cubes form in the last part of the wombat's intestine. Wombats use them to mark territory, and the flat sides stop them rolling away.

facts.s: Bats are blind.
facts.e: All bats can see, and many see well. Many species also use echolocation to hunt in the dark.

facts.s: Tardigrades, or 'water bears', can survive exposure to the vacuum of space.
facts.e: In 2007, tardigrades survived 10 days exposed to space. They can enter a dried-out state that withstands extreme cold, heat and radiation.

facts.s: Some species of bamboo can grow almost a metre in a single day.
facts.e: Some bamboos grow up to about 91 cm in 24 hours, among the fastest growth of any plant.

facts.s: Ostriches bury their heads in the sand when they're scared.
facts.e: Ostriches don't do this. They lie low or run at up to 70 km/h. The myth may come from them turning their eggs in nests dug into the ground.

facts.s: A blue whale's heart can weigh around 180 kg.
facts.e: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived, and its heartbeat can be detected from kilometres away.

facts.s: Koalas spend up to about 20 hours a day sleeping or resting.
facts.e: Their eucalyptus diet is low in nutrients and energy, so they save energy by resting most of the day.

facts.s: The Amazon rainforest is home to around 10% of all known species on Earth.
facts.e: It's the world's largest tropical rainforest, spread across nine countries, and new species are discovered there every year.

facts.s: Honeybees tell each other where to find flowers by dancing.
facts.e: In the 'waggle dance', the angle of the dance shows the direction relative to the Sun and its length shows the distance.

facts.s: In seahorses, the males carry the eggs and give birth.
facts.e: The female places her eggs in the male's pouch, where he fertilises and carries them until hundreds of tiny seahorses are born.

facts.s: People who are bad at something tend to overestimate how good they are at it.
facts.e: This is known as the Dunning–Kruger effect: a lack of skill can also mean a lack of the knowledge needed to judge that skill.

facts.s: People are either 'left-brained' (logical) or 'right-brained' (creative).
facts.e: Some functions are stronger on one side, but large studies find no evidence that people rely on one hemisphere more than the other.

facts.s: Seeing faces in clouds, cars or electrical sockets has a name: pareidolia.
facts.e: Our brains are tuned to detect faces quickly, so they often find them where none exist.

facts.s: Students learn much better when teaching matches their 'learning style' (visual, auditory or kinesthetic).
facts.e: People have preferences, but studies have found little evidence that matching teaching to a 'learning style' improves results.

facts.s: You remember things better if you spread your study sessions out over time.
facts.e: This is called the spacing effect. Reviewing material across several days beats cramming. This app brings back facts you got wrong for the same reason.

facts.s: Most people can hold only around 4 to 7 items in short-term memory at once.
facts.e: That's why phone numbers are split into chunks: grouping information helps memory hold more.

facts.s: After you learn a new word, it suddenly seems to appear everywhere. This feeling has a name.
facts.e: It's called the frequency illusion, or Baader–Meinhof phenomenon. Your attention now notices something that was always there.

facts.s: Sugar makes children hyperactive.
facts.e: Controlled studies have found no effect of sugar on children's behaviour. Parents who believe their child had sugar tend to rate them as more hyperactive.

facts.s: People are less likely to help someone in trouble when other bystanders are present.
facts.e: This is the bystander effect: responsibility feels shared, so each person waits for someone else to act.

facts.s: The brain is about 2% of body weight but uses about 20% of the body's energy.
facts.e: The brain's roughly 86 billion neurons are constantly active, which makes it the most energy-hungry organ for its size.

facts.s: A placebo can help some patients even when they know it's a placebo.
facts.e: Studies of 'open-label' placebos found that some patients, for example with irritable bowel syndrome, reported improvement even after being told the pills were fake.

facts.s: Playing Mozart to babies makes them more intelligent.
facts.e: The 'Mozart effect' study found only a brief, small boost on one kind of puzzle in college students. Later studies did not find lasting effects.

facts.s: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza.
facts.e: The Great Pyramid was finished around 2560 BC and Cleopatra died in 30 BC, about 2,500 years later. The Moon landing came about 2,000 years after her death.

facts.s: The University of Oxford is older than the Aztec Empire.
facts.e: Teaching at Oxford existed by 1096. The Aztec capital Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325.

facts.s: Napoleon Bonaparte was unusually short.
facts.e: Napoleon was about 1.70 m, roughly average for a Frenchman of his time. The myth came partly from confusion between French and British inches, and from British cartoons.

facts.s: Vikings wore horned helmets in battle.
facts.e: There is no evidence of this. The horned-helmet image was popularised in the 19th century, notably by costumes for Wagner's operas.

facts.s: The Ottoman Empire lasted for more than 600 years.
facts.e: It was founded around 1299 and dissolved in 1922. At its height it stretched across south-eastern Europe, western Asia and North Africa.

facts.s: Nalanda, in present-day India, was a great centre of learning for around 700 years, attracting students from across Asia.
facts.e: Nalanda flourished from about the 5th century until around 1200 AD. Its ruins are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

facts.s: The Inca Empire kept records using knotted cords called quipu.
facts.e: Quipus recorded numbers, such as taxes and census data, through the type and position of knots. Whether they also recorded language is still debated.

facts.s: In the Middle Ages, most educated Europeans believed the Earth was flat.
facts.e: Scholars had known the Earth was round since ancient Greece, and medieval scholars agreed. The myth spread mostly in the 19th century.

facts.s: Mansa Musa, a 14th-century ruler of the Mali Empire, is often described as one of the richest people in history.
facts.e: On his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324, he reportedly gave away so much gold in Cairo that its value there fell for years.

facts.s: The Great Fire of London in 1666 destroyed most of the medieval city, but very few deaths were recorded.
facts.e: It burned about 13,200 houses and St Paul's Cathedral, yet only a handful of deaths were recorded. The true number is unknown.

facts.s: The Berlin Wall fell in 1989 and Germany was reunified in 1990.
facts.e: The wall opened on 9 November 1989 and reunification followed on 3 October 1990, now Germany's national day.

facts.s: Some Roman concrete structures, like the Pantheon's dome, have survived for around 2,000 years.
facts.e: The Pantheon's unreinforced concrete dome is still the largest of its kind. Roman concrete may partly heal its own cracks.

facts.s: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built by enslaved people.
facts.e: Evidence from workers' villages and tombs shows that it was built by paid labourers and skilled craftsmen, likely including seasonal workers.

facts.s: Cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation had planned streets and drainage systems over 4,000 years ago.
facts.e: Cities like Mohenjo-daro and Harappa had grid layouts, brick houses, covered drains and public baths. Their script is still undeciphered.

facts.s: A Japanese construction company, Kongō Gumi, operated for over 1,400 years.
facts.e: It was founded in 578 AD to build a Buddhist temple and was run by the same family for centuries before becoming part of another company in 2006.

facts.s: The shortest war in recorded history lasted less than an hour.
facts.e: The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896 ended after about 38 to 45 minutes of British naval bombardment.

facts.s: The Hundred Years' War lasted exactly 100 years.
facts.e: The series of conflicts between England and France lasted 116 years, from 1337 to 1453, with long periods of truce.

facts.s: A Japanese soldier kept fighting in the Philippine jungle until 1974, because he didn't believe World War II had ended.
facts.e: Hiroo Onoda surrendered only when his former commanding officer flew out to formally relieve him of duty.

facts.s: In 1932, Australian soldiers with machine guns fought a 'war' against emus, and largely lost.
facts.e: The 'Great Emu War' tried to cull emus damaging crops in Western Australia. The fast, scattered birds proved very hard to hit.

facts.s: During Christmas 1914, some British and German soldiers stopped fighting and met in no man's land.
facts.e: In the unofficial Christmas truce, soldiers exchanged greetings, food and souvenirs, and some even played football.

facts.s: World War I began in 1918.
facts.e: World War I ran from 1914 to 1918. It began after Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria was assassinated in Sarajevo.

facts.s: At Thermopylae in 480 BC, a small Greek force including 300 Spartans held off a huge Persian army for three days.
facts.e: King Leonidas and his men were eventually outflanked, but the stand became one of history's most famous last stands.

facts.s: At the Battle of Saragarhi in 1897, 21 Sikh soldiers defended their post against thousands of attackers.
facts.e: The soldiers of the 36th Sikhs fought to the last man. 12 September is commemorated as Saragarhi Day.

facts.s: The bloodshed of the Kalinga War led Emperor Ashoka to turn to Buddhism and non-violence.
facts.e: Ashoka's remorse after conquering Kalinga (c. 261 BC) is recorded in his rock edicts. He then spread Buddhist ideas across Asia.

facts.s: The Cold War was a direct full-scale war between the United States and the Soviet Union.
facts.e: The two superpowers never fought each other directly. They competed through an arms race, the space race and proxy wars in other countries.

facts.s: In the 'Pig War' of 1859 between the USA and Britain, the only casualty was a pig.
facts.e: A border dispute over the San Juan Islands escalated after an American farmer shot a British-owned pig. The standoff ended peacefully.

facts.s: China's 19th-century Taiping Rebellion was one of the deadliest conflicts in human history.
facts.e: Estimates of the dead range from about 20 to 30 million, more than in World War I.

facts.s: Paraguay lost a large share of its population in the War of the Triple Alliance (1864–1870).
facts.e: Fighting Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay at once, Paraguay may have lost between a quarter and over half of its people, including most adult men.

facts.s: The Mongol Empire was the largest contiguous land empire in history.
facts.e: Founded by Genghis Khan in 1206, at its height it stretched from Korea to Eastern Europe.

facts.s: One of the first webcams was set up to watch a coffee pot.
facts.e: In 1991, researchers at the University of Cambridge set up a camera so they could check the Trojan Room coffee pot without walking to it. It went online in 1993.

facts.s: Bubble wrap was originally invented as wallpaper.
facts.e: In 1957, two engineers tried to make textured plastic wallpaper. It flopped, but the material later found its use as packaging.

facts.s: Thomas Edison invented the first electric light bulb.
facts.e: Many inventors made incandescent lamps before Edison. His team's achievement was a practical, long-lasting bulb and a power system to run it.

facts.s: Paper, printing, gunpowder and the compass were all invented in China.
facts.e: Known as the Four Great Inventions, they transformed communication, warfare and navigation around the world.

facts.s: In 1947, engineers found a real moth in a computer and recorded it as the 'first actual case of bug being found'.
facts.e: The moth was taped into the Harvard Mark II logbook. The word 'bug' for a technical fault is older, but this is its most famous example.

facts.s: The Wright brothers' first powered flight in 1903 lasted about 12 seconds.
facts.e: Orville Wright flew 37 m (120 ft) at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. Their longest flight that day lasted 59 seconds.

facts.s: Velcro was inspired by burrs that stuck to a dog's fur.
facts.e: Swiss engineer George de Mestral studied burrs under a microscope after a walk with his dog and saw tiny hooks. Velcro was patented in the 1950s.

facts.s: The Internet and the World Wide Web are the same thing.
facts.e: The Internet is the global network of computers. The Web, invented by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989, is one service that runs on it, like email.

facts.s: The QR code was invented in Japan to track car parts.
facts.e: Denso Wave, part of the Toyota group, created the QR code in 1994. It can be read quickly from any angle.

facts.s: Kenya was a world pioneer of mobile-phone money with M-Pesa, launched in 2007.
facts.e: M-Pesa let people send and store money by text message, without a bank account. It spread across Africa and beyond.

facts.s: The microwave oven was invented after a radar engineer noticed a chocolate bar melting in his pocket.
facts.e: Percy Spencer of Raytheon noticed the effect while working near a magnetron in the 1940s. Early microwave ovens were taller than a person.

facts.s: The @ sign was chosen for email addresses in 1971.
facts.e: Ray Tomlinson picked @ for the first networked email system because it meant 'at' and wasn't used in names.

facts.s: The QWERTY keyboard layout was designed for typewriters in the 1870s.
facts.e: Christopher Latham Sholes developed it for early typewriters. It stuck around long after the machines it was built for disappeared.

facts.s: Paper money was first widely used in China.
facts.e: Paper money called jiaozi was issued during the Song dynasty, over 1,000 years ago. Europe adopted banknotes centuries later.

facts.s: On the island of Yap, giant stone discs were used as money.
facts.e: Some rai stones are several metres wide. Ownership could change without moving the stone, because everyone remembered who owned it.

facts.s: During Zimbabwe's hyperinflation in 2008, prices roughly doubled every day.
facts.e: Inflation peaked at about 79.6 billion percent per month. Zimbabwe printed a 100 trillion dollar note.

facts.s: Most modern currencies are backed by gold.
facts.e: Today's currencies are 'fiat money': their value comes from government decree and public trust, not gold. The US dollar left the gold standard in 1971.

facts.s: The word 'salary' is linked to the Latin word for salt.
facts.e: It comes from the Latin 'salarium', related to 'sal' (salt). The popular story that Roman soldiers were paid in salt is disputed.

facts.s: The worst hyperinflation ever recorded was in Hungary in 1946, when prices doubled about every 15 hours.
facts.e: The pengő became so worthless that Hungary printed a 100 quintillion (10²⁰) pengő banknote.

facts.s: The Dutch 'Tulip mania' of the 1630s is often cited as one of the first recorded speculative bubbles.
facts.e: Rare tulip bulbs reportedly sold for more than a house before prices suddenly collapsed in 1637. Historians debate how widespread the damage was.

facts.s: Every country in the European Union uses the euro.
facts.e: 20 of the 27 EU countries use the euro. Others, such as Sweden, Poland and Denmark, keep their own currencies.

facts.s: India's UPI system handles billions of digital payments every month.
facts.e: The Unified Payments Interface lets people pay instantly by phone. Even small street vendors accept it with a QR code.

facts.s: Sweden is one of the world's most cashless societies.
facts.e: Cash is used in only a small fraction of payments in Sweden. Many shops and even some banks don't handle cash at all.

facts.s: The first general-purpose charge card, Diners Club, appeared in 1950.
facts.e: According to legend, it was inspired by a businessman who forgot his wallet at a restaurant.

facts.s: Before alarm clocks were common, people called 'knocker-uppers' were paid to wake workers by tapping on their windows.
facts.e: They used long poles or pea-shooters to reach upper windows. The job lasted in some British towns until the 1970s.

facts.s: 'Computer' used to be a job title for people who did calculations by hand.
facts.e: Human computers, often women, calculated everything from astronomy tables to rocket trajectories, including at NASA in the 1950s and 60s.

facts.s: Almost all lighthouses today are automated, so the job of lighthouse keeper has nearly disappeared.
facts.e: Keepers once lived at remote lighthouses to keep the lamps lit. Automation replaced most of them during the 20th century.

facts.s: Mumbai's dabbawalas deliver well over 100,000 home-cooked lunches every working day.
facts.e: Using bicycles, trains and a colour-coded system of marks, they deliver with remarkable accuracy and carry the empty boxes home again.

facts.s: Most doctors today recite the ancient Hippocratic Oath word for word.
facts.e: The original oath swears by Greek gods. Medical schools today use modern versions, such as the Declaration of Geneva, if they use an oath at all.

facts.s: Professional mourners, people paid to weep at funerals, have existed in many cultures.
facts.e: Professional mourning is recorded in ancient Egypt, ancient Rome and the Bible, and is still practised in parts of China and elsewhere.

facts.s: Most US air traffic controllers face a mandatory retirement age of 56.
facts.e: The rule reflects how demanding and high-stakes the job is. Controllers must also start training before about age 31.

facts.s: Iceland trialled shorter working weeks for public workers from 2015 to 2019, with wellbeing improving and productivity maintained.
facts.e: After the trials, most of Iceland's workforce gained the right to negotiate shorter hours.

facts.s: Only a few hundred people have ever passed the Master Sommelier exam for wine experts.
facts.e: The exam includes identifying wines by taste alone, without seeing the bottle. Many candidates attempt it several times.

facts.s: Organised firefighting services began only in the 20th century.
facts.e: Ancient Rome created the Vigiles in 6 AD: thousands of men who fought fires and patrolled the streets at night.

facts.s: Many airlines have the pilot and co-pilot eat different meals.
facts.e: If one meal causes food poisoning, the other pilot should still be fit to fly the plane.

facts.s: Before refrigerators, cutting and shipping ice from frozen lakes was a major global industry.
facts.e: In the 19th century, ice from New England and Norway was shipped as far as India and the Caribbean.

facts.s: Treating zero as a number in its own right, with rules for adding, subtracting and multiplying, was developed in India.
facts.e: Brahmagupta set out rules for calculating with zero in 628 AD. The concept travelled through the Islamic world to Europe.

facts.s: There are more ways to order a shuffled deck of 52 cards than there are atoms on Earth.
facts.e: 52! is about 8 × 10⁶⁷, far more than the roughly 10⁵⁰ atoms on Earth. A well-shuffled deck is almost certainly in an order never seen before.

facts.s: In a room of just 23 people, there's about a 50% chance that two of them share a birthday.
facts.e: This is the birthday paradox. With 23 people there are 253 possible pairs, and with 70 people the chance rises above 99.9%.

facts.s: 0.999… (with the 9s repeating forever) is slightly less than 1.
facts.e: 0.999… is exactly equal to 1. For example, 1/3 = 0.333…, and three times that is 0.999… = 3/3 = 1.

facts.s: Fibonacci numbers appear in nature, for example in the spirals of sunflower seeds.
facts.e: Sunflower heads and pine cones often have 34 and 55, or 55 and 89, spirals in each direction. These are consecutive Fibonacci numbers.

facts.s: The digits of pi eventually repeat in a pattern.
facts.e: Pi is irrational: its decimal expansion never ends and never falls into a repeating pattern. It has been computed to trillions of digits.

facts.s: There are infinitely many prime numbers, which was proven over 2,000 years ago.
facts.e: Euclid's elegant proof: multiply any finite list of primes together and add 1. The result has a prime factor that isn't on the list.

facts.s: All infinite sets are the same size.
facts.e: Georg Cantor proved that some infinities are bigger than others. For example, there are more real numbers than whole numbers.

facts.s: In theory, folding a sheet of paper in half 42 times would make it thick enough to reach the Moon.
facts.e: Doubling 0.1 mm 42 times gives about 440,000 km, more than the 384,000 km to the Moon. In practice, paper can't be folded that many times.

facts.s: A 'googol' is 1 followed by 100 zeros, and it inspired the name Google.
facts.e: The word was coined in 1920 by a nine-year-old, the nephew of mathematician Edward Kasner. Google's founders adapted the spelling.

facts.s: In the Monty Hall problem, switching doors doubles your chance of winning the car.
facts.e: Your first pick wins 1/3 of the time, so switching wins 2/3 of the time. Many mathematicians refused to believe it at first.

facts.s: Srinivasa Ramanujan, a largely self-taught mathematician from India, produced nearly 3,900 results.
facts.e: He worked with G. H. Hardy at Cambridge. Mathematicians are still exploring the formulas in his notebooks.

facts.s: The equals sign (=) was invented in 1557.
facts.e: Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde introduced it because 'no two things can be more equal' than a pair of parallel lines.

facts.s: A circle has 360 degrees because of a law of nature.
facts.e: 360 is a convention, probably inherited from Babylonian astronomy and its base-60 number system. Mathematicians often use radians instead.

facts.s: Fermat's Last Theorem remained unproven for more than 350 years.
facts.e: Pierre de Fermat claimed a proof in a margin in 1637. Andrew Wiles finally proved it in 1994.

facts.s: Christianity and Islam are the two largest religions in the world by number of followers.
facts.e: Christianity has around 2.3 billion followers and Islam around 1.9 billion. Hinduism is third, with over 1 billion.

facts.s: Hinduism is often described as the oldest living major religion, with roots more than 3,000 years old.
facts.e: Its earliest texts, the Vedas, were composed more than 3,000 years ago. Hinduism has no single founder.

facts.s: Some Jain monks sweep the ground in front of them as they walk, to avoid harming insects.
facts.e: Jainism teaches ahimsa, non-violence towards all living beings, so strictly that many Jains avoid root vegetables to spare tiny organisms.

facts.s: The Golden Temple in Amritsar serves free meals to tens of thousands of people every day.
facts.e: Its langar, a community kitchen run largely by volunteers, feeds anyone regardless of religion, caste or background. Everyone sits together on the floor.

facts.s: Buddhists worship the Buddha as an all-powerful creator god.
facts.e: The Buddha was a human teacher, Siddhartha Gautama, who taught a path to end suffering. Buddhism does not centre on a creator god.

facts.s: Shinto, Japan's indigenous religion, has no single founder and no single holy book.
facts.e: Shinto centres on kami, spirits found in nature, places and ancestors, and is practised at about 80,000 shrines.

facts.s: Zoroastrianism, one of the world's oldest religions, is still practised by the Parsi community in India.
facts.e: Parsis migrated from Persia to India over a thousand years ago. Famous Parsis include the Tata family and Freddie Mercury.

facts.s: Judaism, Christianity and Islam are called 'Abrahamic religions'.
facts.e: All three trace their origins to the figure of Abraham and share many prophets and stories.

facts.s: During Ramadan, many Muslims fast from dawn until sunset for about a month.
facts.e: The fast is broken each evening with a meal called iftar. Ramadan ends with the celebration of Eid al-Fitr.

facts.s: The Bahá'í Faith, founded in 19th-century Persia, teaches the unity of all religions.
facts.e: Its world centre, with famous terraced gardens, is in Haifa and Acre in Israel.

facts.s: Many people in Japan take part in both Shinto and Buddhist traditions.
facts.e: A common saying is that people are born Shinto and die Buddhist: births are celebrated at shrines, while funerals are usually Buddhist.

facts.s: 'Atheist' and 'agnostic' mean exactly the same thing.
facts.e: An atheist doesn't believe in any god. An agnostic holds that whether gods exist is unknown or unknowable. Some people are both.

facts.s: Lalibela in Ethiopia has 11 medieval churches carved out of solid rock.
facts.e: Carved downward into the ground around the 12th and 13th centuries, they are still active places of worship.

facts.s: Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument in the world, was first built as a Hindu temple.
facts.e: Built in the 12th century and dedicated to Vishnu, it gradually became a Buddhist temple. It appears on Cambodia's flag.

facts.s: The 'trolley problem' asks whether it's right to divert a runaway trolley so it kills one person instead of five.
facts.e: Philosophers and psychologists use it to explore when, if ever, it's acceptable to harm one person to save more.

facts.s: Versions of the 'Golden Rule' (treat others as you want to be treated) appear in many religions and philosophies worldwide.
facts.e: It appears in Confucianism, Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism, Christianity and Islam, among others.

facts.s: Utilitarianism judges actions by whether they produce the greatest good for the greatest number.
facts.e: Developed by Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill, it's the basis for many cost–benefit decisions in public policy.

facts.s: Socrates wrote many books setting out his philosophy.
facts.e: Socrates wrote nothing. We know his ideas mainly through his students, especially Plato.

facts.s: The 'Ship of Theseus' puzzle asks whether an object that has had every part replaced is still the same object.
facts.e: The question applies to everything from bands with no original members to the human body, whose cells are constantly replaced.

facts.s: Confucius taught that a harmonious society depends on proper relationships, such as respect for parents and elders.
facts.e: Confucian ideas about family, education and good government have shaped East Asian cultures for over 2,000 years.

facts.s: The Southern African philosophy of 'Ubuntu' is often summed up as 'I am because we are'.
facts.e: Ubuntu stresses community, compassion and shared humanity. It was often cited by Nelson Mandela and Desmond Tutu.

facts.s: Philosopher Peter Singer argued that if you'd ruin your shoes to save a drowning child, you should also give to save distant strangers.
facts.e: His 1972 essay 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' helped inspire the effective altruism movement.

facts.s: Kant argued that lying is wrong even to a murderer asking where your friend is hiding.
facts.e: Kant held that moral duties like honesty don't depend on consequences, a view still debated today.

facts.s: Machiavelli advised rulers to always be kind and honest.
facts.e: In The Prince (1532), Machiavelli wrote that it's safer for a ruler to be feared than loved, and that deception can be necessary.

facts.s: John Rawls asked people to design a fair society without knowing which position in it they would end up in.
facts.e: Rawls called this the 'veil of ignorance'. He argued it would lead people to protect the worst-off.

facts.s: Stoic philosophers such as Marcus Aurelius taught people to focus on what is within their control.
facts.e: Marcus Aurelius, a Roman emperor, wrote his Stoic reflections in a private journal now known as Meditations.

facts.s: The Arthashastra is an ancient Indian treatise on statecraft, economics and military strategy.
facts.e: It's traditionally attributed to Chanakya (Kautilya), adviser to the Maurya Empire's founder.

facts.s: Chess probably originated in India.
facts.e: Its ancestor, chaturanga, was played in India around the 6th century AD. The game spread through Persia to the Arab world and Europe.

facts.s: There are more possible chess games than atoms in the observable universe.
facts.e: Claude Shannon estimated about 10¹²⁰ possible games, compared with about 10⁸⁰ atoms in the observable universe.

facts.s: Basketball was invented by a Canadian.
facts.e: James Naismith, a Canadian-born teacher, invented it in 1891 in Springfield, Massachusetts, using peach baskets as hoops.

facts.s: An astronaut has hit golf balls on the Moon.
facts.e: Alan Shepard hit two golf balls on the Moon during Apollo 14 in 1971, using a club head attached to a sample-collection tool.

facts.s: Kabaddi, a fast contact sport where a raider must hold their breath while chanting, originated in ancient India.
facts.e: It's Bangladesh's national sport and is hugely popular across South Asia, with professional leagues.

facts.s: According to tradition, the ancient Olympic Games began in 776 BC.
facts.e: They were held every four years at Olympia in honour of Zeus, for over 1,000 years.

facts.s: Tug of war has never been an Olympic sport.
facts.e: Tug of war was part of the Olympic Games from 1900 to 1920.

facts.s: An AI first beat a top professional player at the board game Go in 2016.
facts.e: DeepMind's AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol 4–1. Go has so many possible positions that this was expected to take another decade.

facts.s: A Test cricket match can last up to five days and still end in a draw.
facts.e: Test cricket is the longest format of the sport. A draw happens when time runs out before a result is reached.

facts.s: Sepak takraw is like volleyball, but players can only use their feet, knees, chest and head.
facts.e: It's popular across Southeast Asia, and players perform acrobatic overhead kicks to spike the ball.

facts.s: Snakes and ladders originated in ancient India as a game about morality.
facts.e: Called Moksha Patam, it used ladders to represent virtues and snakes to represent vices. British players brought it to Europe.

facts.s: Tetris was created by a Soviet software engineer in 1984.
facts.e: Alexey Pajitnov developed it in Moscow. Its name combines 'tetra' (four, the number of squares in each piece) and tennis, his favourite sport.

facts.s: The first modern Olympic Games were held in Paris in 1896.
facts.e: They were held in Athens in 1896, honouring the ancient Greek games. Paris hosted the second, in 1900.

facts.s: A Rubik's Cube has over 43 quintillion possible positions.
facts.e: That's 43,252,003,274,489,856,000 positions. Hungarian inventor Ernő Rubik created the cube in 1974.

facts.s: Any scrambled Rubik's Cube can be solved in 20 moves or fewer.
facts.e: This was proved in 2010 using about 35 CPU-years of donated computer time. The number is nicknamed 'God's Number'.
facts.w: Optimal solutions for the Rubik's Cube

facts.s: Beethoven composed his Ninth Symphony when he was almost completely deaf.
facts.e: At its premiere in 1824, Beethoven reportedly had to be turned around to see the audience applauding.

facts.s: The Taj Mahal was built by Emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal.
facts.e: Construction began in 1632 and involved around 20,000 workers. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

facts.s: The Statue of Liberty was designed and built in the United States.
facts.e: It was a gift from France, designed by Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi with an iron framework engineered by Gustave Eiffel, built in Paris and shipped in pieces.

facts.s: India produces more feature films each year than any other country.
facts.e: India produces well over 1,500 films a year in many languages: Bollywood (Hindi), Tollywood (Telugu), Kollywood (Tamil) and more.

facts.s: In Indian classical music, many ragas are traditionally linked to particular times of day.
facts.e: A raga is a melodic framework for improvisation. Some are meant for dawn, others for evening or night, and some for particular seasons.

facts.s: The Mona Lisa was stolen from the Louvre in 1911.
facts.e: An Italian handyman, Vincenzo Peruggia, hid it for over two years. The theft made it the most famous painting in the world.

facts.s: Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling in just a few weeks.
facts.e: It took him about four years, from 1508 to 1512, working mostly standing up on scaffolding with his head tilted back.

facts.s: BTS were the first all-South Korean act to top the US Billboard Hot 100.
facts.e: Their song 'Dynamite' reached number 1 in 2020, a milestone in K-pop's global rise.

facts.s: Hokusai's 'The Great Wave off Kanagawa' is a woodblock print, so many original copies exist.
facts.e: Made around 1831, it was printed from carved wooden blocks. Thousands of impressions were made, and museums around the world own early ones.

facts.s: Mozart and Beethoven were close friends of the same age.
facts.e: Mozart was born in 1756 and Beethoven in 1770. They may have met briefly in Vienna in 1787, but they were never close friends.

facts.s: There is a famous piece of music in which the performers play no notes at all.
facts.e: In John Cage's 4′33″ (1952), the musicians sit silently, and the 'music' is the ambient sound of the room.

facts.s: The Terracotta Army includes around 8,000 life-size soldier figures, buried with China's first emperor.
facts.e: Farmers digging a well discovered it in 1974. Each soldier's face is different.

facts.s: Kintsugi is the Japanese art of repairing broken pottery with gold, highlighting the cracks rather than hiding them.
facts.e: It reflects the idea that breakage and repair are part of an object's history, not something to disguise.

facts.s: Reggae music originated in Jamaica in the late 1960s.
facts.e: Bob Marley brought reggae to the world, and UNESCO added it to its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2018.
